analysis.one_liner: Ends the legal exemption allowing 55-and-older housing communities to exclude families with children.
analysis.headline: Solely sponsored by Sen. Booker with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee on September 19, 2024, and never received a hearing or vote before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The federal Fair Housing Act makes it illegal to refuse to sell or rent housing to families because they have children. Since 1988, however, an exemption — known as the Thurmond amendment — has let "housing for older persons," such as 55-and-over communities, turn families with children away. This bill would delete that exemption, making age-restricted communities follow the same anti-discrimination rules as everyone else. It never advanced past its introduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Families with children who are turned away from age-restricted housing — renters and buyers who today can be excluded from these communities solely because of their children.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes paragraph (4) of Section 807(b) of the Fair Housing Act, removing the legal carve-out for "housing for older persons."

With the carve-out gone, the Fair Housing Act's general prohibition on familial-status discrimination — refusing to rent or sell to people because they have children — would apply to age-restricted communities, because the bill's only operative change is striking that paragraph from the exemption list.

analysis.who_pays: Developers and operators of 55-and-older communities would lose the right to market and sell homes exclusively to older adults, and some older residents who chose those communities specifically to live without children would lose that option.

drawbacks.text: The exemption was a deliberate compromise added in 1988: it lets older adults maintain communities designed around their needs, and many residents chose those homes precisely because children do not live there. Repeal would end that choice rather than regulate it.

The age-restricted housing industry has argued that its products serve real demand from older adults, and full repeal could reduce or eliminate a housing type many seniors rely on, rather than simply opening more doors to families.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would open a meaningful housing option to families with children, but it does so by eliminating an exemption that supports a housing form chosen by many older adults; the cost falls on seniors who prefer child-free communities and on the industry that serves them, and the bill offered no transition or middle-ground approach.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which never took it up, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Fair Future Act on September 19, 2024, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No further action was taken: the action history shows no hearings, no committee vote, and no floor action before the 118th Congress ended.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor, so the bill entered its first and only committee referral with zero support beyond its author.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of 55-and-older communities keep the legal right to exclude families with children, and families remain barred from that housing stock.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Age-restricted housing operators and existing residents

for.name: Sen. Cory Booker
for.role: U.S. Senator, New Jersey; bill's only sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and filed it for referral, but recruited no cosponsors before the session ended.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the Fair Housing Act
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on September 19, 2024, and held no hearing, markup, or vote on it for the rest of the session.

sides.party_line_note: There is no vote or floor debate to break down by party; the only recorded supporter was a Democrat, with zero cosponsors of either party [S3].

industries.industry: Age-restricted (55+) housing developers and community operators
industries.note: Repealing the exemption would take away these communities' legal ability to market homes only to older adults, ending the adults-only character their business model and resale appeal depend on. Families with children would gain the housing option the industry currently excludes.
